```{python}
ax.plot(skills, kap_curve, "-o", ms=3, color="#3b6ea5", label=r"Cohen's $\kappa$")
ax.axhline(0.76, ls=":", color="grey", lw=1)
ax.annotate(r"reported $\kappa=0.76$", (0.03, 0.79), fontsize=8, color="grey")
ax.scatter([0.42, 0.42], [lazyj[1], lazyj[3]], marker="X", s=70, color="#a03030", zorder=5)
ax.plot([0.42, 0.42], [lazyj[3], lazyj[1]], color="#a03030", lw=1.2, ls="--")
ax.annotate("lazy judge: raw agreement\nabove the curve, kappa below", (0.42, 0.54),
            textcoords="offset points", xytext=(12, -6), fontsize=8,
            color="#a03030", ha="left")
ax.set_xlabel("judge skill (probability of naming the true label)")
ax.set_ylabel("score")
ax.set_title("Raw agreement is inflated; kappa is not")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower right")

ax = axes[1]
names = ["prior\nonly", "outcome\nsymptom\n(Bayes)",
         "interaction\nlabel\n($\\kappa$=0.76)", "interaction\nlabel\n(perfect)"]
vals = [acc_prior, acc_outcome, acc_localized, 1.0]
bars = ax.bar(names, vals, color=["#999999", "#b5651d", "#3b6ea5", "#2f5d3a"])
for b, v in zip(bars, vals):
    ax.text(b.get_x() + b.get_width() / 2, v + 0.015, f"{v:.3f}", ha="center", fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.12)
ax.set_ylabel("expected repair success")
ax.set_title("What the interaction trace buys you")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

**Reading the reliability table.** The prevalence is sharply skewed: the heaviest single cell carries 0.326 of the mass and the collision mass is $S = 0.146$, so by @eq-498-keff the effective number of labels is 6.8, not 30. A taxonomy that looks like a 30-way classification behaves, for agreement purposes, like a seven-way one. The four graded judges confirm @eq-498-kappa-recovers-skill to Monte Carlo precision: skills of 0.34, 0.51, 0.64, and 0.76 yield $\kappa$ of 0.340, 0.506, 0.637, and 0.757, while their raw agreements run 0.436, 0.579, 0.690, and 0.793, each inflated by roughly $(1-a)S$ as the closed form predicts (at $a = 0.76$ the prediction is $0.76 + 0.24 \times 0.146 = 0.795$ against a measured 0.793). The two degenerate raters show why the correction is not cosmetic. A rater that ignores the trajectory entirely and always answers with the most common cell agrees with the human on 32.7% of items and scores $\kappa = 0.000$ exactly, because for a constant rater $p_o = p_e = p_{\max}$ and the numerator of @eq-498-kappa vanishes identically. More pointedly, the lazy judge, which has genuine skill 0.42 but falls back on the majority cell whenever it is unsure, posts raw agreement of 0.609 against judge B's 0.579 while scoring $\kappa = 0.477$ against judge B's 0.506. On raw agreement the lazy judge looks better; on $\kappa$ it is worse, and $\kappa$ is right, because the extra agreement was purchased with prior mass rather than with evidence.

Set against that backdrop, $\kappa = 0.76$ over a sparse taxonomy is a strong result and should still be read soberly. On the conventional Landis and Koch bands it falls in the "substantial" range (0.61 to 0.80) and short of "almost perfect" (0.81 to 1.00), and those bands are interpretive convention rather than theorem. The operational reading is @eq-498-kappa-recovers-skill run backwards: roughly three quarters of the judge's category assignments reflect structure shared with the human annotator, and something close to one item in four would still be filed differently by a person. That is good enough to support the paper's claim that the categories capture shared structure rather than annotator-specific preference, and it is not good enough to auto-label a benchmark unsupervised. It is also worth stating the standard caveat that $\kappa$ is not comparable across studies with different label prevalences, precisely because $p_e$ depends on the marginals, so a $\kappa$ measured on one failure corpus does not transfer unexamined to another.

**Reading the repair-assignment table.** The four repair targets are unevenly loaded by construction: harness engineering owns three of the six components and 0.617 of the failure mass, against 0.171 for environment redesign, 0.144 for post-training, and 0.069 for benchmark repair. That sets a punishing baseline, since a team that reflexively blames the harness and never looks at a trace is right 0.617 of the time. The Bayes-optimal outcome-level policy of @eq-498-bayes-repair, which is the best that any decoding of the visible symptom can achieve, reaches only 0.690. Four of the five symptoms point at harness engineering with posteriors between 0.563 and 0.964, and only "task left incomplete" flips the recommendation, to post-training, and even then with posterior 0.427, which is to say the recommendation it produces is more likely wrong than right. The information accounting says the same thing without the anecdote: $H(\text{repair}) = 1.534$ bits, $H(\text{repair} \mid \text{symptom}) = 1.129$ bits, so the symptom carries $I = 0.405$ bits, only 26.4% of what the interaction label supplies. Feeding those numbers into @eq-498-fano gives a floor of 0.064 on the outcome-level error rate against an actual 0.310; the bound is valid but loose here, and its value is qualitative rather than numerical, certifying that no decoder whatsoever can reach zero error while more than a bit of conditional entropy remains.

The comparison that matters is the last two rows. A localized label supplied by a judge no better than the $\kappa = 0.76$ one reported in the paper assigns the correct repair 0.867 of the time, against the outcome-level ceiling of 0.690, and a perfect localized label reaches 1.000 by construction. An imperfect interaction label therefore closes about 57% of the gap between the outcome-level ceiling and perfection, which is the practical case for the taxonomy: you do not need flawless localization to beat outcome-level evaluation, you only need localization that is better than chance on the fault side, because the fault side is the coordinate the outcome cannot see at all.

The kappa computation is worth writing out on its own, both because it is three lines and because those three lines are the difference between an evaluation that reports something and one that reports something meaningful. The Python tab runs; the Julia and Rust tabs are illustrative.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Python

```{python}
#| label: code-498-kappa
import numpy as np


def kappa_from_confusion(confusion):
    """Cohen's kappa from a raw count matrix: rows are rater one's labels,
    columns are rater two's. Returns (p_o, p_e, kappa)."""
    P = np.asarray(confusion, dtype=float)
    P = P / P.sum()
    p_o = float(np.trace(P))                        # observed agreement
    p_e = float(P.sum(axis=1) @ P.sum(axis=0))      # chance agreement
    return p_o, p_e, (p_o - p_e) / (1.0 - p_e)


# Three cells of the taxonomy, human labels down the rows, judge labels across.
counts = [[420, 30, 10],
          [55, 120, 25],
          [15, 20, 55]]
p_o, p_e, kappa = kappa_from_confusion(counts)
print(f"raw agreement    p_o = {p_o:.3f}")
print(f"chance agreement p_e = {p_e:.3f}")
print(f"Cohen kappa          = {kappa:.3f}")
```

## Julia

```julia
using LinearAlgebra

"""Cohen's kappa from a raw count matrix. Returns (p_o, p_e, kappa)."""
function kappa_from_confusion(confusion::AbstractMatrix{<:Real})
    P = confusion ./ sum(confusion)
    p_o = sum(diag(P))                               # observed agreement
    row = vec(sum(P, dims = 2))
    col = vec(sum(P, dims = 1))
    p_e = dot(row, col)                              # chance agreement
    return p_o, p_e, (p_o - p_e) / (1 - p_e)
end

counts = [420 30 10; 55 120 25; 15 20 55]
p_o, p_e, kappa = kappa_from_confusion(counts)
println("raw agreement    p_o = ", round(p_o, digits = 3))
println("chance agreement p_e = ", round(p_e, digits = 3))
println("Cohen kappa          = ", round(kappa, digits = 3))
```

## Rust

```rust
/// Cohen's kappa from a raw count matrix. Returns (p_o, p_e, kappa).
fn kappa_from_confusion<const K: usize>(confusion: &[[f64; K]; K]) -> (f64, f64, f64) {
    let total: f64 = confusion.iter().flatten().sum();
    let mut p_o = 0.0;
    let mut row = [0.0f64; K];
    let mut col = [0.0f64; K];
    for i in 0..K {
        for j in 0..K {
            let p = confusion[i][j] / total;
            if i == j {
                p_o += p; // observed agreement
            }
            row[i] += p;
            col[j] += p;
        }
    }
    let p_e: f64 = (0..K).map(|i| row[i] * col[i]).sum(); // chance agreement
    (p_o, p_e, (p_o - p_e) / (1.0 - p_e))
}

fn main() {
    let counts = [[420.0, 30.0, 10.0], [55.0, 120.0, 25.0], [15.0, 20.0, 55.0]];
    let (p_o, p_e, kappa) = kappa_from_confusion(&counts);
    println!("raw agreement    p_o = {p_o:.3}");
    println!("chance agreement p_e = {p_e:.3}");
    println!("Cohen kappa          = {kappa:.3}");
}
```

:::

That small example is worth one more look, because it lands on a striking coincidence. Its raw agreement is 0.793, identical to judge D's raw agreement over the 30-cell space, and yet its $\kappa$ is 0.606 against judge D's 0.757. The difference is entirely in the chance term: 0.476 here on three heavily unbalanced labels, against 0.147 there. Two evaluations reporting the same headline agreement can describe raters of quite different quality, and only @eq-498-kappa distinguishes them.

**What to take from this section.** The taxonomy is a coordinate system, and the argument for adopting it is not that its 41 modes are the right 41. It is that outcome-level labels are provably non-invertible with respect to the repair decision (the identifiability proposition), that the coordinate they are missing is the fault side rather than more granular symptom vocabulary, and that recovering that coordinate is cheap enough to be worth doing even imperfectly. The chapter's own catalogue makes the point better than an abstract argument does: Section 6.1 and @sec-498-role-drift describe failures on the *same edge* that differ only in which endpoint is at fault, and every mitigation this chapter has proposed silently presumed an answer to that question. Diversifying system prompts is a harness-side repair; it does nothing if the model's distribution is the degenerate one. Anchoring the role effect is a model-side repair; it does nothing if the harness never supplied a coherent role prompt to begin with. Combined with the closing recommendation of @sec-498-role-drift, the operational rule is short: **record the interaction trace, label failures by edge and fault side, and report per-module role fidelity alongside end-task accuracy**, because a benchmark score tells you that your multi-agent system is broken and never once tells you whom to send the ticket to.
